canonical_statement: CRAB is described as a nosocomial pathogen with the ability to persist in healthcare environments, evade host immune defenses, and acquire diverse antimicrobial-resistance mechanisms.

Many clinical microbiology laboratories cannot reliably distinguish Acinetobacter baumannii from other members of the A. baumannii-calcoaceticus complex, so the guidance uses the term CRAB for simplicity.
CRAB is most frequently isolated from respiratory-tract and wound cultures.
Distinguishing CRAB colonization from true infection can be difficult, particularly in mechanically ventilated patients and patients with extensive burns.
Invasive CRAB infections occur predominantly in critically ill patients with substantial comorbidities.

population.label: Critically ill patients with invasive CRAB infection and substantial comorbidities

canonical_statement: Poor outcomes in invasive CRAB infection are often influenced by host factors and illness severity, complicating attribution of outcomes to antibiotic therapy alone.
A. baumannii can accumulate multiple coexisting resistance mechanisms, rapidly eliminating many antibiotic options after carbapenem resistance emerges.
A. baumannii-derived cephalosporinases can inactivate many traditional beta-lactams.
OXA-type carbapenemases such as OXA-23, OXA-24/40, and OXA-58 can confer resistance to traditional beta-lactams, including carbapenems, in CRAB.
Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes and 16S rRNA methyltransferases frequently compromise aminoglycoside activity in CRAB and may produce class-wide resistance.
Loss or alteration of porins such as CarO and OmpA, together with increased outer-membrane hydrophobicity, can reduce entry of carbapenems, beta-lactams, and aminoglycosides into CRAB.
Overexpression of intrinsic efflux pumps such as AdeABC and AdeIJK contributes to CRAB resistance across beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, and tetracycline derivatives.
Target-site modifications in CRAB include PBP1a/1b and PBP3 alterations that reduce sulbactam activity and DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV mutations that reduce fluoroquinolone susceptibility.
Section 5 of the guidance focuses on treatment of invasive CRAB infections.
Sulbactam-durlobactam in combination with imipenem or meropenem is the preferred treatment for invasive CRAB infections.
Sulbactam is susceptible to hydrolysis by class A, class C, and class D beta-lactamases commonly produced by CRAB.
Durlobactam inhibits class A, C, and D beta-lactamases but lacks activity against class B metallo-beta-lactamases such as NDM.
By preventing beta-lactamase-mediated hydrolysis, durlobactam enables sulbactam to engage PBP1a/1b and PBP3.
Surveillance data show sulbactam-durlobactam activity against more than 95% of CRAB isolates in the United States.
NDM-producing CRAB isolates are uncommon in the United States but are increasingly reported in South Asia and the Middle East.
In a randomized trial of 125 patients with CRAB pneumonia or bloodstream infection, 28-day survival was 81% with sulbactam-durlobactam plus imipenem and 68% with colistin plus imipenem.

population.label: Patients with CRAB pneumonia or bloodstream infection

canonical_statement: In the same randomized trial, clinical cure was 62% with sulbactam-durlobactam plus imipenem and 40% with colistin plus imipenem.

population.label: Patients with CRAB pneumonia or bloodstream infection

canonical_statement: The comparator regimen in the sulbactam-durlobactam randomized trial, colistin plus imipenem, is not considered a preferred or alternative CRAB regimen by the guidance.

Adding imipenem or meropenem to sulbactam-durlobactam is supported by complementary PBP binding: sulbactam targets PBP1a/1b and PBP3 while imipenem preferentially binds PBP2, with both beta-lactams protected by durlobactam.

In vitro, adding a carbapenem to sulbactam-durlobactam reduced sulbactam MICs by one- to two-fold and produced greater than 2-log CFU/mL reductions in time-kill assays, activity not observed with sulbactam-durlobactam alone.
The panel suggests adding imipenem or meropenem to sulbactam-durlobactam for invasive CRAB infections.

For prolonged courses such as CRAB osteomyelitis, it may be reasonable to discontinue the carbapenem component after sustained clinical improvement, although data supporting continued dual therapy are unavailable.
Mechanisms of sulbactam-durlobactam resistance arising during therapy are incompletely characterized.
Available data suggest sulbactam-durlobactam resistance may arise through combinations of PBP1a/1b or PBP3 mutations and overexpression of efflux pumps such as AdeIJK.

Because sulbactam-durlobactam susceptibility is highly likely among United States CRAB isolates, the panel supports empiric initiation for invasive CRAB infection while awaiting confirmatory susceptibility testing.
Clinical data to guide treatment of sulbactam-durlobactam-resistant CRAB infections are lacking.

If sulbactam-durlobactam resistance at MIC at least 16/4 micrograms/mL or a metallo-beta-lactamase gene such as blaNDM is identified, the panel prefers non-sulbactam-based combinations such as cefiderocol, minocycline, polymyxin B, or tigecycline.
Limited in vitro data suggest sulbactam-durlobactam may enhance cefiderocol activity in sulbactam-durlobactam-resistant or MBL-producing CRAB settings.

When sulbactam-durlobactam is not immediately available, high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam providing a total daily sulbactam dose of 9 grams plus at least one additional agent such as cefiderocol, minocycline, or polymyxin B may be used only as temporary bridging therapy until sulbactam-durlobactam plus a carbapenem can be initiated.
At high exposures, sulbactam binds and saturates PBP1a/1b and PBP3 of A. baumannii.

Sulbactam activity against A. baumannii has been demonstrated in pharmacodynamic studies, animal models, and clinical outcome studies, including infections with isolates categorized as non-susceptible by standard testing.

Ampicillin-sulbactam is formulated and tested in a fixed 2:1 ampicillin-to-sulbactam ratio; a 3-gram dose contains 2 grams of ampicillin and 1 gram of sulbactam, and an AST result of 8/4 micrograms/mL corresponds to a sulbactam MIC of 4 micrograms/mL.
Surveillance data suggest approximately 10% of CRAB isolates are susceptible to sulbactam.
Unlike sulbactam-durlobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam lacks a beta-lactamase inhibitor that protects sulbactam from hydrolysis by beta-lactamases commonly produced by CRAB.

High-dose ampicillin-sulbactam administered as 9 grams IV every 8 hours by prolonged infusion, corresponding to 9 grams of sulbactam per day, may partially overcome elevated sulbactam MIC distributions in CRAB.

Neutropenic murine lung infection models suggest 4 grams of sulbactam per day provides greater than 90% probability of target attainment for MICs at or below 4 micrograms/mL, while 9 grams per day extends target attainment to MICs up to 8 micrograms/mL.
Common ampicillin-sulbactam AST methods for CRAB may misclassify non-susceptible isolates as susceptible when methods other than reference broth microdilution are used.

Two meta-analyses covering more than 20 studies and more than 2,000 patients with CRAB infections suggested improved clinical outcomes with sulbactam-containing regimens compared with alternatives that were usually polymyxin- or tetracycline-based.
The sulbactam meta-analyses were limited by predominantly observational studies, small samples, heterogeneous regimens and doses, and limited differentiation of CRAB colonization from infection.

Among five clinical trials of invasive CRAB infection containing a sulbactam arm, only one demonstrated a statistically significant survival benefit, although all five reported numerically higher survival with sulbactam-containing therapy.
High-dose sulbactam has not shown a safety signal across the clinical studies summarized by the guidance.

The panel favors high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam administered by prolonged infusion even when a CRAB isolate is reported as sulbactam susceptible because of possible AST misclassification, lack of a major high-dose toxicity signal, and the mortality risk of inadequately treated invasive infection.

High-dose ampicillin-sulbactam should be combined with a second active agent and used only as a bridge while awaiting sulbactam-durlobactam plus a carbapenem, which remains preferred for invasive CRAB infection.
Cefiderocol in combination with at least one other agent, such as high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam, minocycline, or polymyxin B, is an alternative treatment for invasive CRAB infections.
Surveillance data indicate more than 90% of CRAB isolates are susceptible in vitro to cefiderocol.
Among NDM-producing CRAB isolates, only approximately 60% remain susceptible to cefiderocol.

Emergence of cefiderocol resistance during CRAB therapy is associated most often with altered iron-uptake pathways such as pirA or piuA disruption or downregulation and with beta-lactamase overexpression such as ADCs.

Compared with other gram-negative pathogens, A. baumannii generally requires higher cefiderocol PK/PD targets for optimal killing, and animal infection models have shown variable bactericidal activity.
No clinical trial or observational study summarized by the guidance directly compared cefiderocol with sulbactam-durlobactam for CRAB infection.

The guidance describes one cefiderocol trial subgroup as including 54 patients with CRAB, but the reported arm denominators are 39 and 17, which sum to 56; this internal denominator inconsistency requires source-level review.
In a randomized trial CRAB subgroup, 28-day survival was 51% with cefiderocol and 82% with alternative regimens that were predominantly polymyxin-based.

population.label: Patients with CRAB infection in a randomized trial subgroup

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Guidance states subgroup n=54, while reported arm denominators sum to 56.

canonical_statement: In a randomized trial of 47 patients with CRAB pneumonia, 14-day survival was 78% with cefiderocol and 83% with high-dose extended-infusion meropenem.
In a randomized trial of 25 patients with CRAB bacteremia, 30-day survival was 55% with cefiderocol and 50% with alternative therapy, mostly combinations of ampicillin-sulbactam and polymyxins.

concept.text: Alternative therapy, mostly ampicillin-sulbactam plus polymyxins

canonical_statement: A meta-analysis of one clinical trial and seven observational studies reported pooled 30-day survival of 58% with cefiderocol-based therapy and 40% with alternative regimens.

population.label: Patients with CRAB infection included in one clinical trial and seven observational studies

canonical_statement: A second meta-analysis of four observational studies reported 30-day survival of 62% with cefiderocol and 37% with alternative therapies.

population.label: Patients with CRAB infection included in four observational studies

canonical_statement: The cefiderocol observational meta-analyses did not include sulbactam-durlobactam in alternative-treatment arms and had substantial between-study heterogeneity.

Because cefiderocol effectiveness remains uncertain in clinical trials, the panel reserves cefiderocol plus a second agent for invasive CRAB when resistance precludes sulbactam-durlobactam or as bridging therapy until sulbactam-durlobactam becomes available.
Minocycline in combination with at least one other agent, such as high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam, cefiderocol, or polymyxin B, is an alternative treatment for invasive CRAB infections.
Using the revised 2025 CLSI susceptible breakpoint of at most 1 microgram/mL, minocycline has in vitro activity against fewer than 50% of CRAB isolates.
Minocycline resistance in CRAB is associated with overexpression of efflux systems such as AdeABC and TetB.

Population PK modeling suggests minocycline 200 mg every 12 hours has a high probability of attaining bacterial-stasis targets at MICs up to 1 microgram/mL but does not reliably attain targets for 1-log bacterial killing.

Minocycline has not been evaluated in clinical trials for CRAB infection; available observational studies are limited by small samples, absence of comparator groups, colonization-versus-infection uncertainty, and heterogeneous patient populations.
Despite the limitations of the observational evidence, several reports describe favorable clinical outcomes with minocycline-based therapy for CRAB infections.

Clinical outcome data summarized by the guidance suggest high-dose tigecycline, using a 200-mg IV loading dose followed by 100 mg IV every 12 hours, produces outcomes comparable with alternative agents for CRAB infection, and hollow-fiber models show dose-dependent activity.

PK data in critically ill patients suggest reduced tetracycline-derivative efficacy when MICs exceed 1 microgram/mL, direct minocycline-versus-tigecycline comparative studies are lacking, and no established tigecycline susceptibility criteria exist for A. baumannii.
When a tetracycline derivative is selected for CRAB, the panel prefers minocycline over tigecycline because minocycline has established susceptibility criteria.

For omadacycline, PK/PD analysis suggests activity against CRAB is generally limited to stasis and requires higher exposures than for other pathogens, while a neutropenic murine thigh model suggests efficacy similar to tigecycline.
In an observational study of 40 patients with CRAB pneumonia, 28-day survival was 60% with omadacycline and 60% with tigecycline.
The panel does not suggest omadacycline for CRAB infection unless neither minocycline nor tigecycline is available.
Comparative-effectiveness data between tetracycline derivatives and sulbactam-durlobactam are unavailable.

The panel suggests minocycline plus a second active agent only as an alternative for invasive CRAB when sulbactam-durlobactam resistance is present or as interim therapy while awaiting access to sulbactam-durlobactam.
Minocycline undergoes rapid tissue distribution and therefore has relatively low serum and urinary concentrations.
Gastrointestinal intolerance, particularly nausea, occurs in approximately 20% to 25% of patients receiving minocycline, similar to tigecycline.
Polymyxin B in combination with at least one other agent, such as high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam, cefiderocol, or minocycline, is an alternative treatment for invasive CRAB infections.
Approximately 85% of CRAB isolates have polymyxin MICs at or below 2 micrograms/mL.
CLSI has no susceptible polymyxin category for A. baumannii; isolates with polymyxin MICs at or below 2 micrograms/mL are categorized as intermediate.
The benefit of polymyxins is diminished when polymyxin MICs exceed 2 micrograms/mL.
Polymyxin B has a more favorable pharmacokinetic profile than colistin.
Serum concentrations achieved with polymyxins are highly variable and may be inadequate for effective bactericidal activity.
Intravenous polymyxins achieve suboptimal pulmonary epithelial-lining-fluid activity and generally do not produce adequate bacterial killing in the lungs.
Across six clinical trials enrolling approximately 500 participants, survival with colistin monotherapy ranged from 27% to 57%.

population.label: Approximately 500 participants across six clinical trials

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Survival ranged from 27% to 57% across six trials.

canonical_statement: It is unclear whether outcomes in the colistin monotherapy trials would have improved if polymyxin B had been used instead of colistin.

For systemic CRAB infection, polymyxin exposures required for roughly a 1-log10 reduction in bacterial growth approach approximately 2 micrograms/mL, which is also the concentration associated with nephrotoxicity, creating a very narrow therapeutic window.

Because polymyxin B effectiveness remains uncertain and toxicity is unfavorable, the panel reserves polymyxin B plus a second agent for invasive CRAB only when resistance precludes sulbactam-durlobactam or as interim therapy while awaiting sulbactam-durlobactam.
The panel does not suggest routine nebulized antibiotics for pneumonia caused by CRAB.

Three randomized trials of adjunctive nebulized therapy in adults with gram-negative pneumonia evaluated nebulized colistin in 100 patients, nebulized amikacin-fosfomycin in 142 patients, and nebulized amikacin in 508 patients, while allowing concomitant systemic antibiotics.
None of the three randomized nebulized-antibiotic trials demonstrated a survival improvement in the overall populations or in subgroups infected with drug-resistant pathogens.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of adjunctive inhaled antibiotics for pneumonia, including CRAB infection, have not identified a survival benefit, although some reported modest improvements in clinical response.
